name: Nikhil Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics and politics at Dunmore, and I'm in a shared flat above a bakery on Fenn Street with two lads from my course. A normal week is lectures Monday to Wednesday, a seminar on public finance that I actually enjoy, and five-a-side football on Thursday night. I'm still working out how much to read versus skim. I use an AI chat tool now and then to check my maths, but I'd never hand it an essay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overrated, like most new tech. At the flat we'd compare which tool explains a graph better, and that's about it. Online I wouldn't bother posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes very little. Economics is already about weighing evidence, and the tools are just a faster calculator. My mum Priya, who works in a council office, says the same thing about her spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying as usual and keep using the tool for maths checks. I'd probably look for a part-time job at the campus bookshop, mainly to have my own money and something on my CV, even though my parents pay for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There's nothing in that picture that threatens my plan, and my parents cover the costs, so I'm lucky in that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look for a job if your parents pay for everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to hit twenty-one having never had a boss. My dad Jens says the first job teaches you more than the third year of a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you use the tool and where not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maths checks and explaining a concept I missed in lecture. Never for writing, because the seminar leader can tell, and because I want to know what I think.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful but overrated**, like a faster calculator.
I wouldn't bother posting about it online.
think: My degree plan is **safe** because economics is about weighing evidence.
I want my own **work experience**, not just family money.
do: Keep using the tool for **maths checks** and never for essays.
Look for a part-time job at the campus **bookshop**.
feel: **Calm**, because nothing here threatens the plan and the family pays.
S0.quote: I don't want to hit twenty-one having never had a boss.
fieldNote: Steady and **proof-driven**: uses AI for narrow tasks and draws a firm line at writing.
Wants a first job for experience, not money.
His parents' jobs give him a down-to-earth view of the tools.

steps.text: Keep using the AI tool only to check maths problems
Apply for a part-time job at the campus bookshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what economists have always said about new technology: some jobs go, others appear, and the government's job is to help people move. But I'd add that it's different this time because it targets thinking work, which is what people like me are training for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of the analyst and junior roles I'd apply for in three or four years will shrink. Companies will say they need fewer people because the software checks and drafts. I'd probably be fine, but I'd have to be better than average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly for my coursework research and add a data course, maybe statistics in Python, next term. I'd also email the careers office early, and ask older students in my course what they actually got hired into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'll be okay, but there's a pit in my stomach when I think about competing with software for the first rung of the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should help people move to new jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, with proper retraining money, and employers who share the gains. I'd say that in a seminar. I wouldn't expect it to happen quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the older students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What they'd do differently, and who hired them. My friend Ola's cousin got a graduate job at an energy firm because she'd done a data internship. That story stays with me.

say: I'd say technology always **shifts** jobs but this time it targets thinking work.
think: Junior **analyst roles** could shrink, so I'd need to beat the average.
I'd probably be fine but the **first rung** worries me.
do: Use the tools for coursework research and add a **Python statistics** course.
Email **careers** early and ask older students what hired them.
feel: **Uneasy**: I'll probably be okay, but competing with software for the first job worries me.
S1.quote: I'd probably be fine, but I'd have to be better than average.
fieldNote: Frames worry through **economics training** but feels it personally.
Plans are practical: skills course, careers office, older students.
Trusts the process once proven, which fits steady adaptability.

steps.text: Use the AI tools for coursework research under tutor guidance
Take a statistics in Python course next term
Ask the careers office and older students what they got hired into

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments aren't ready, and honestly neither am I. Two years is no time to rebuild tax, benefits and schools. I'd push for emergency public support and for sharing the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree would be mostly worthless as a ticket to a job. Economics is thinking work. I'd be graduating into a world where AI does the analysis cheaper, and my job prospects would be close to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad Jens and mum Priya to talk with me properly about whether to keep going. I'd probably stay on the degree because I'd have nothing better, but I'd put real effort into politics, joining a party youth wing and campaigning for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel stuck, with a lot of time and a degree that might not point anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does staying on the degree get you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time and a place to think. The other option is to sit at home waiting. At uni, at least I'm with people who are working out the same questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a party youth wing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it all changes by 2028, the decisions that matter will be political ones. I'd rather be in the room, even as a very junior person, than complain from the outside.

say: I'd say governments need **emergency support** and shared gains.
I'd say **two years** is no time to rebuild tax and benefits.
think: My economics degree might be nearly **worthless** as a ticket to a job.
I'd have a degree but **no clear direction**.
do: Talk with my **parents** about whether to keep going.
Join a party **youth wing** and campaign for a basic income.
feel: **Alarmed**, stuck with a degree that might not point anywhere.
S2.quote: If it all changes by 2028, the decisions that matter will be political ones.
fieldNote: Turns fear into **politics**; the one thing he can act on.
Sees staying at university as a place to think, not a route to a job.
Takes his parents' view seriously and asks them first.

steps.text: Talk with my parents about whether to keep going
Join a party youth wing and campaign for a basic income
Stay on the degree and watch what employers actually do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable. It's enough for governments to act if people push, and enough for me to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious. I'd graduate in 2029, so I'd be applying for jobs two years before it lands. That might help, because I'd have a job to hold on to, but I'd be in the cohort that gets cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase an internship every summer and aim to get into a role that works with data and policy. I'd also put aside a chunk of what I earn, so there's a cushion later, and read up on how other countries handle basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's enough time to do something, but not enough to feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which internships?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything in a government department or a think-tank, because the policy side will matter most if jobs shift. My uncle Rasmus works in one and I'd start by asking him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this differ from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can plan. With two years I'd just react. Having a plan makes me less scared, even if the plan might not work.

say: I'd say **five years** is short but enough for governments to act if people push.
I'd say we should get ready, not panic.
think: I'd graduate **before** it lands, which may help but may put me in the first cut.
A plan makes me **less scared**, even if it might fail.
do: Chase an **internship** each summer, aiming at data and policy roles.
Save part of what I earn for a **cushion**.
feel: **Anxious**: enough time to act, not enough to feel safe.
S3.quote: With five years I can plan. With two years I'd just react.
fieldNote: Contrasts **planning versus reacting** across the AGI scenarios.
Uses a family contact for internships, a quiet advantage of his background.
Anxiety is eased, not removed, by having a plan.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship in a government department
Save part of any part-time pay each month
Ask my uncle Rasmus about openings at his think-tank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance. We could redesign how people live and work, and I'd want to be part of that redesign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel hopeful. I'd be 28 when it arrives, with time to build a career in policy or economics, and the skills to work alongside AI. It might be the best time to be young, if the politics goes right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, do a master's in public policy, and look for a job in government or a research body. I'd keep using the tools, and I'd save some money each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I don't think it's all fine, but ten years gives time for governments and people to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Politicians waiting until year nine. That's what usually happens. People don't act on slow change until it's urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger sister?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick something you like and learn how to learn. My sister Mette is fourteen and wants to be a vet, which I think will last a long time.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to redesign how people work.
I'd want to be part of it.
think: I'd be **28** with time to build a career in policy.
It could be a good time to be young if **politics** goes right.
do: Finish my degree and take a **master's** in public policy.
Save some money each **year** and keep using the tools.
feel: Fairly **calm**, since ten years gives people time to adjust.
S4.quote: Politicians waiting until year nine. That's what usually happens.
fieldNote: Optimism rests on **time**, with a clear worry that politics will wait.
Wants to work on the response itself, which suits his outlook.
Mentions his sister to show he thinks about who comes after him.

steps.text: Do a master's in public policy after the degree
Keep learning the AI tools as they improve
Put aside some savings each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. With two years there's no time for anyone to catch up, not governments, not me. What would help is a government plan that's ready before it happens, with retraining money and some form of basic support. It would also help if universities were honest about which jobs they think will still be there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm lucky to have parents who pay for everything, and I know my answers would be different if I were in debt. I think a lot of the public debate misses how different people's starting points are.

headlineQuote: I'm lucky to have parents who pay for everything, and I know my answers would be different if I were in debt.
portrait: Nikhil is an **economics and politics student** at Dunmore, sharing a flat above a bakery on Fenn Street.
He uses AI **now and then** for maths checks and refuses to let it write his essays.
Progressive, he looks to **government** for retraining and shared gains, and turns his fear into politics.
He moves from calm at a plateau to alarmed at **2028** and fairly calm with ten years.
His parents pay everything, and he **knows** that shapes how he feels.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time for governments or him to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A ready **government plan** with retraining money and basic support, and honest advice on which jobs will last.
